title: Policy structure, insureds, limits and other insurance
summary: Follow Tony's Pizza through one Detroit week: the parts of a policy, who is insured, deductibles, sharing a loss, and limits.
objectives: Tell declarations, insuring agreement, conditions and exclusions apart
Tell named, first named and additional insureds apart
Split a loss between insurers: primary and excess, pro rata, equal shares
Apply deductibles, split and combined single limits, and policy period and territory

scenes.title: Roll the DICE: the parts of Tony's policy
scenes.src: Memory hook mn_core-15; IRMI glossary: declarations, insuring agreement, exclusion, endorsement; ISO CP 00 10 10 12; ISO HO 00 03 05 11

spots.label: Declarations
spots.text: Who, where, when and how much: the named insureds, the address and location, the policy period and the limits.

spots.label: Insuring agreement
spots.text: The insurer's promise to pay. It starts broad, and the exclusions and definitions narrow it.

spots.label: Conditions
spots.text: The rules both sides follow, such as duties after a loss, cancellation, and how other insurance is shared.

spots.label: Exclusions
spots.text: What is not covered: certain hazards, perils, property or circumstances. A homeowner's 2011 HO-3, for example, excludes earth movement and flood.

spots.label: Definitions
spots.text: Words in quotation marks have special meanings, spelled out in the policy's Definitions section.

spots.label: Endorsements
spots.text: Forms the insurer issues to change the policy: they broaden or restrict coverage, clarify it, or add insureds or locations.

beats.say: Where do I even start?

beats.text: Roll the DICE: Declarations, Insuring agreement, Conditions, Exclusions. Definitions explain the words in quotes; endorsements change the game.
beats.say: Roll the DICE: Declarations, Insuring agreement, Conditions, Exclusions. Definitions explain the words in quotes; endorsements change the game.

scenes.title: Who is insured on Tony's policy?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: named insured, first named insured, additional insured; ISO IL 00 17 11 98; question core-053
scenes.plain: The insured listed first in the declarations. Pays the premium, and gets cancellation notices and return premiums.
scenes.example: Tony and his grandma co-own the pizzeria, and the policy names both: two named insureds. Tony is listed first: he pays the premium and gets the notices and refunds.
scenes.exam: Named insured: anyone named in the policy. Trap: only the first named pays the premium and gets notices. Additional insured: added on request.

beats.text: Who's insured? Tony and his grandma co-own the pizzeria, and the policy names both: two named insureds.
beats.say: Who's insured? Tony and his grandma co-own the pizzeria, and the policy names both: two named insureds.

beats.text: Tony is listed first in the declarations: the first named insured. He pays the premium and gets cancellation notices and return premiums.
beats.say: Tony is listed first in the declarations: the first named insured. He pays the premium and gets cancellation notices and return premiums.

beats.text: Tony also rents a Midtown takeout counter. That landlord isn't named, but Tony can ask to add him as an additional insured.
beats.say: Tony also rents a Midtown takeout counter. That landlord isn't named, but Tony can ask to add him as an additional insured.

beats.text: On the exam, a named insured is anyone named in the policy.
beats.say: On the exam, a named insured is anyone named in the policy.

beats.text: The trap: under the 1998 common policy conditions, only the first named insured pays the premium and gets notices.
beats.say: The trap: under the nineteen ninety-eight common policy conditions, only the first named insured pays the premium and gets notices.

scenes.title: The landlord wants in
scenes.src: ISO IL 00 17 11 98, B. Changes; IRMI glossary: additional insured; ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. II; core-bas-22
scenes.ask: How does Tony add the landlord?

draw.text: My lease says I go on your policy!

beats.text: That afternoon, the Midtown landlord stops by. His lease says he must be on Tony's policy. What does Tony do?
beats.say: That afternoon, the Midtown landlord stops by. His lease says he must be on Tony's policy. What does Tony do?

options.label: Write his name in with a pen
options.fail: His policy's terms can be amended only by an endorsement the insurer issues. Tony may change them only with the insurer's consent.

beats.text: Tony pens the landlord's name in. Sorry, Tony: a pen can't change a policy.
beats.say: Tony pens the landlord's name in. Sorry, Tony: a pen can't change a policy.

options.label: Tell him he's covered as the landlord
options.fail: A landlord isn't an insured just for being the landlord. He becomes one when added at the named insured's request: an additional insured.

beats.text: Then why isn't my name on it?
beats.say: Then why isn't my name on it?
beats.speaker: Landlord

beats.text: Being Tony's landlord doesn't make him an insured.
beats.say: Being Tony's landlord doesn't make him an insured.

draw.text: Then why isn't my name on it?

options.label: Ask Dana to add him by endorsement
options.win: The insurer's endorsement adds him as an additional insured, at Tony's request. A project owner can be added the same way.

beats.text: Done! The insurer issued an endorsement.
beats.say: Done! The insurer issued an endorsement.

beats.text: Now the landlord is an additional insured, added at Tony's request.
beats.say: Now the landlord is an additional insured, added at Tony's request.

reveal.text: Only the insurer's endorsement changes Tony's policy. Tony, the first named insured, can change it only with the insurer's consent.
reveal.say: Only the insurer's endorsement changes Tony's policy. Tony, the first named insured, can change it only with the insurer's consent.

scenes.title: Grease fire! What does Tony do?
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: common policy conditions, exclusion, unilateral contract; ISO CP 00 10 10 12, E.3; core-bas-17, core-bas-18

beats.text: Tuesday, a grease fire scorches Tony's kitchen. It's out, and nobody's hurt. What does Tony do now?
beats.say: Tuesday, a grease fire scorches Tony's kitchen. It's out, and nobody's hurt. What does Tony do now?

options.label: Check the exclusions
options.fail: Exclusions list what is not covered. The duties after a loss, like prompt notice, are conditions.

beats.text: Page after page of what isn't covered. Tony sweats. Wrong list.
beats.say: Page after page of what isn't covered. Tony sweats. Wrong list.

options.label: Check the conditions
options.win: Conditions are the rules both sides follow, including the duties after a loss, like giving prompt notice.

beats.text: Found it: duties after loss. One duty: give the insurer prompt notice. Tony calls right away.
beats.say: Found it: duties after loss. One duty: give the insurer prompt notice. Tony calls right away.

options.label: Mention it at renewal, no rush
options.fail: The conditions' duties after loss include prompt notice. Waiting months breaks that duty, and that can put the claim at risk.

beats.text: Months later, at renewal, Tony finally mentions the fire. That's not prompt notice.
beats.say: Months later, at renewal, Tony finally mentions the fire. That's not prompt notice.

reveal.text: Rules after a loss, like prompt notice, live in the conditions.
reveal.say: Rules after a loss, like prompt notice, live in the conditions.

scenes.title: The adjuster's math: deductible, then limit
scenes.src: ISO CP 00 10 10 12 (2012 BPP), D, Examples 1-2; IRMI: deductible; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. B; core-bas-27 to 29

goal.text: Find the loss where the insurer pays exactly $59,750.
goal.done: $60,000 loss pays $59,750: deductible off the loss.

draw.text:
Equipment damage: $70,000
Limit (most it pays): $60,000
Deductible: $250
No coinsurance penalty (next lesson)
2011 HO, two deductibles: only the highest applies

beats.text: Wednesday, the adjuster tallies $70,000 of fire damage to Tony's ovens and kitchen equipment. His 2012 property form insures them: limit $60,000, deductible $250, no coinsurance penalty.
beats.say: Wednesday, the adjuster tallies seventy thousand dollars of fire damage to Tony's ovens and kitchen equipment. His twenty twelve property form insures them: limit sixty thousand dollars, deductible two hundred fifty dollars, no coinsurance penalty.

beats.text: The deductible, the first slice Tony pays himself, comes off the loss, not the limit. That leaves $69,750, over the limit, so the insurer pays $60,000.
beats.say: The deductible, the first slice Tony pays himself, comes off the loss, not the limit. That leaves sixty-nine thousand seven hundred fifty dollars, over the limit, so the insurer pays sixty thousand dollars.

beats.text: Your turn: which loss pays exactly $59,750?
beats.say: Your turn: which loss pays exactly fifty-nine thousand seven hundred fifty dollars?

reveal.text: A loss of $60,000. The full limit takes $60,250.
reveal.say: A loss of sixty thousand dollars. The full limit takes sixty thousand two hundred fifty dollars.

reveal.text: That form takes the deductible once per occurrence, even when one fire hits two buildings with separate limits.
reveal.say: That form takes the deductible once per occurrence, even when one fire hits two buildings with separate limits.

reveal.text: Under the 2011 homeowners forms, if two or more deductibles apply to the same loss, only the highest applies.
reveal.say: Under the twenty eleven homeowners forms, if two or more deductibles apply to the same loss, only the highest applies.

scenes.title: Inside the policy's time and place?
scenes.src: ISO PP 00 01 09 18 (2018 PAP), Part F; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. Q; ISO CP 00 90 07 88, H; core-bas-23 to 26

cards.text: Rosa, insured under the 2018 personal auto policy, drives from Lansing to Toronto, Canada.
cards.why: The 2018 PAP's territory is the U.S., its territories or possessions, Puerto Rico and Canada. Toronto is inside.

cards.text: Next spring, Rosa drives the same car to Mexico.
cards.why: Mexico is not part of the 2018 PAP's policy territory.

cards.text: Sam has a 2011 HO-3. A storm hits his house on the policy period's last day. He reports it the next morning.
cards.why: Section I applies only to loss that occurs during the policy period. The storm hit inside it, so the later report date is not the test.

cards.text: The bakery next door let its commercial property policy end on March 1. A fire starts there on March 10.
cards.why: Under the 1988 commercial property conditions, the loss must start during the policy period. This fire started after it ended.

cards.text: Rosa's covered car rides a cargo boat between ports in the U.S. and Puerto Rico.
cards.why: The 2018 PAP also covers a covered auto while it is being transported between ports of those places.

beats.text: Meanwhile, Dana's other clients ask: when, and where?
beats.say: Meanwhile, Dana's other clients ask: when, and where?

beats.text: Can I drive to Toronto? Or Mexico?
beats.say: Can I drive to Toronto? Or Mexico?

beats.text: When: under these auto, homeowners and commercial property forms, the loss must happen, or start, in the policy period, not just get reported then.
beats.say: When: under these auto, homeowners and commercial property forms, the loss must happen, or start, in the policy period, not just get reported then.

beats.text: Where: Rosa's 2018 personal auto policy covers the United States, its territories or possessions, Puerto Rico and Canada, plus shipping between their ports. Not Mexico.
beats.say: Where: Rosa's twenty eighteen personal auto policy covers the United States, its territories or possessions, Puerto Rico and Canada, plus shipping between their ports. Not Mexico.

beats.text: Your turn: inside or outside?
beats.say: Your turn: inside or outside?

reveal.text: Two tests, then: the dates, and for auto and commercial property, the map.
reveal.say: Two tests, then: the dates, and for auto and commercial property, the map.

reveal.text: The 1988 commercial property conditions list the same places.
reveal.say: The nineteen eighty-eight commercial property conditions list the same places.

scenes.title: Two policies, one loss: splitting the check
scenes.src: Adapted from hook mn_core-18; IRMI glossary; ISO CP 00 90 07 88, G.1; ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. IV Cond. 4.c; core-bas-30

draw.text: Same amounts until a limit runs out or the loss is paid
Not allowed by one? Split by limits
Nonconcurrency: same exposure, policies that don't match
Not a way to share a loss

beats.text: Thursday lunch at a Coney Island: one check, two friends, like two insurers sharing one loss.
beats.say: Thursday lunch at a Coney Island: one check, two friends, like two insurers sharing one loss.

beats.text: Primary and excess: one friend pays first; the other covers only what's left above a stated amount or the primary.
beats.say: Primary and excess: one friend pays first; the other covers only what's left above a stated amount or the primary.

beats.text: Pro rata, or contribution by limits: pay by your appetite, your limit. Limits of $300,000 and $200,000 pay three-fifths and two-fifths. On a loss of $100,000, that's $60,000 and $40,000.
beats.say: Pro rata, or contribution by limits: pay by your appetite, your limit. Limits of three hundred thousand dollars and two hundred thousand dollars pay three-fifths and two-fifths. On a loss of one hundred thousand dollars, that's sixty thousand dollars and forty thousand dollars.

beats.text: Equal shares, the method in the CGL, a business liability policy: everyone chips in the same until a wallet runs dry. In other words, they pay the same amounts until a limit runs out or the loss is paid. If any policy doesn't permit equal shares, they split by limits.
beats.say: Equal shares, the method in the C G L, a business liability policy: everyone chips in the same until a wallet runs dry. In other words, they pay the same amounts until a limit runs out or the loss is paid. If any policy doesn't permit equal shares, they split by limits.

beats.text: And don't confuse these with nonconcurrency: policies on the same exposure that don't match, like different inception and expiration dates. Picture one building with two policies: January 1 to January 1, and April 1 to April 1. That's nonconcurrency, not a way to share a loss.
beats.say: And don't confuse these with nonconcurrency: policies on the same exposure that don't match, like different inception and expiration dates. Picture one building with two policies: January first to January first, and April first to April first. That's nonconcurrency, not a way to share a loss.

scenes.title: The adjuster's puzzle: one claim, two CGLs
scenes.src: ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. IV Cond. 4.c (Method of sharing); IRMI glossary: contribution by equal shares; question core-038

draw.text: $250,000 claim. Both permit equal shares. Who pays what?

beats.text: Friday, an adjuster has two CGL policies on one claim. Limits: $100,000 and $300,000.
beats.say: Friday, an adjuster has two C G L policies on one claim. Limits: one hundred thousand dollars and three hundred thousand dollars.

beats.text: The claim's $250,000, and both permit equal shares. Who pays what?
beats.say: The claim's two hundred fifty thousand dollars, and both permit equal shares. Who pays what?

options.label: Each insurer pays $125,000
options.fail: Equal shares means equal amounts only until a policy has paid its limit. A $100,000 policy can never pay $125,000.

beats.text: Impossible: the small policy's whole limit is $100,000.
beats.say: Impossible: the small policy's whole limit is one hundred thousand dollars.

options.label: The big one pays $150,000
options.win: Equal shares: each pays the same until a limit is used up. Totals: $100,000 and $150,000.

beats.text: Each pays $100,000, using up the small limit. The big one adds the last $50,000, for $150,000 in all.
beats.say: Each pays one hundred thousand dollars, using up the small limit. The big one adds the last fifty thousand dollars, for one hundred fifty thousand dollars in all.

options.label: The big one pays $187,500
options.fail: Contribution by limits applies only if some other policy doesn't permit equal shares. Here, both do.

beats.text: That's pro rata, the backup method. By limits, the small one pays $62,500, and the big one pays $187,500.
beats.say: That's pro rata, the backup method. By limits, the small one pays sixty-two thousand five hundred dollars, and the big one pays one hundred eighty-seven thousand five hundred dollars.

beats.text: Both policies permit equal shares, so it's out.
beats.say: Both policies permit equal shares, so it's out.

reveal.text: Equal shares: alike until a limit is used up. The trap: $187,500, the big policy's share by limits.
reveal.say: Equal shares: alike until a limit is used up. The trap: one hundred eighty-seven thousand five hundred dollars, the big policy's share by limits.

scenes.title: Tony's CGL: per occurrence, and per year
scenes.src: ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. III and Sec. V def. 16.a; IRMI glossary: per occurrence limit, general aggregate limit

draw.text: Each occurrence limit: one cap for all of them

beats.text: Back at Tony's: his CGL has an each occurrence limit, the most paid for one occurrence, however many people claim.
beats.say: Back at Tony's: his C G L has an each occurrence limit, the most paid for one occurrence, however many people claim.

beats.text: Each policy year also has aggregates, caps on the year's total. There's a general one, for things like a slip inside the shop, and one for products-completed operations.
beats.say: Each policy year also has aggregates, caps on the year's total. There's a general one, for things like a slip inside the shop, and one for products-completed operations.

beats.text: For Tony, that's injury away from his premises from his product, like takeout pizza that makes someone sick at home.
beats.say: For Tony, that's injury away from his premises from his product, like takeout pizza that makes someone sick at home.

scenes.title: Split limits: Person, People, Property
scenes.src: Memory hook mn_core-20; IRMI glossary: split limits, combined single limits; ISO PP 00 01 09 18, Part A; core-bas-36
scenes.plain: Three separate caps per accident: one person's injuries, all injuries, and all property damage.
scenes.example: A driver with 50/100/25 limits is liable for a crash: two people hurt ($70,000 and $40,000) and $30,000 of property damage. Paid: $50,000, $40,000 and $25,000.
scenes.exam: Cap each person first, then the accident. A combined single limit is one limit for injury and damage together.

beats.text: Now a textbook auto liability example, set outside Michigan, where the rules differ. Read split limits as Person, People, Property. This example uses the 2018 personal auto policy.
beats.say: Now a textbook auto liability example, set outside Michigan, where the rules differ. Read split limits as Person, People, Property. This example uses the twenty eighteen personal auto policy.

beats.text: 50, 100, 25: $50,000 per person, $100,000 for all injuries, $25,000 for all property damage. Those are three separate caps per accident.
beats.say: Fifty, one hundred, twenty-five: fifty thousand dollars per person, one hundred thousand dollars for all injuries, twenty-five thousand dollars for all property damage. Those are three separate caps per accident.

beats.text: The driver is legally liable for two injuries: $70,000 and $40,000. Person one caps at $50,000. Person two gets all $40,000, so injuries pay $90,000.
beats.say: The driver is legally liable for two injuries: seventy thousand dollars and forty thousand dollars. Person one caps at fifty thousand dollars. Person two gets all forty thousand dollars, so injuries pay ninety thousand dollars.

beats.text: Property damage of $30,000 pays $25,000. Total: $115,000.
beats.say: Property damage of thirty thousand dollars pays twenty-five thousand dollars. Total: one hundred fifteen thousand dollars.

beats.text: Cap each person first, then the accident. A combined single limit is one big bucket for all of it: one limit for injury and damage together.
beats.say: Cap each person first, then the accident. A combined single limit is one big bucket for all of it: one limit for injury and damage together.

scenes.q: An auto policy has a $300,000 combined single limit. The insured is liable for $200,000 of injury to one person and $50,000 of property damage. It pays:
scenes.why: One limit for injury and property damage together, with no per-person cap. $250,000 fits inside $300,000.

beats.text: Quick check: one big bucket. What does the insurer pay?
beats.say: Quick check: one big bucket. What does the insurer pay?

reveal.text: $250,000: no per-person cap, and it all fits.
reveal.say: Two hundred fifty thousand dollars: no per-person cap, and it all fits.

items: DICE: declarations, insuring agreement, conditions, exclusions
First named insured: pays the premium, gets notices and refunds
The deductible comes off the loss; the limit still caps the payment
Equal shares: alike till a limit runs out. Pro rata: by limits
Split limits: cap each person first, then the accident

draw.text: Next time, I read the conditions before the fire!

beats.text: What a week! Roll the DICE: declarations, insuring agreement, conditions, exclusions. The first named insured pays the premium and gets notices and refunds. The deductible comes off the loss; the limit still caps the payment.
beats.say: What a week! Roll the DICE: declarations, insuring agreement, conditions, exclusions. The first named insured pays the premium and gets notices and refunds. The deductible comes off the loss; the limit still caps the payment.

beats.text: Equal shares pay alike until a limit runs out; pro rata pays by limits. Split limits cap each person first, then the accident.
beats.say: Equal shares pay alike until a limit runs out; pro rata pays by limits. Split limits cap each person first, then the accident.
